blocks.content: You have probably solved the same problem twice without realizing it.
Different project. Different code. Same underlying structure. You figured it out the first time, forgot how, and built it again from scratch.
Design patterns exist so you never have to do that.

A design pattern is a named, proven solution to a problem that keeps appearing in software. Not a library. Not copy-paste code. Just a battle-tested blueprint with a name that every developer understands.
Say "I used the Observer pattern here" and any developer on your team instantly knows the structure no lengthy explanation needed.
They are the collected wisdom of developers who hit the same walls you are hitting. And wrote down what worked.
The chapters ahead will walk you through the most important ones when to use them, and when to leave them alone.
1. What Are Design Patterns?
A design pattern is a reusable solution to a problem that keeps showing up in software design. Not finished code. Not a library. Just a proven blueprint you adapt to your situation.
Real-World Analogy: A Recipe
A recipe doesn't hand you a finished meal. It gives you a repeatable process tested, refined, and reliable. You still cook it yourself, but you're not guessing from scratch.
Design patterns work the same way. They hand you a proven approach, not a finished solution. You adapt it to your codebase, your language, your situation.
The result? Less reinventing. Less guessing. More confidence.
2. Why Should You Use Design Patterns?
blocks.text: 2. Why Should You Use Design Patterns?

blocks.content: Design patterns provide proven, reusable solutions to common software design problems.
They improve code maintainability, scalability, and make communication between developers easier.
1. Reusability: Stop solving the same problem twice

Patterns are proven solutions you can apply again and again. Someone already figured out the best way to handle a single shared instance, or swap behaviors at runtime. You just use it. Less thinking from scratch. More building on what works.
2. Maintainability: Clean today, easy to fix tomorrow

When code follows a pattern, every piece has a clear job. Nothing overlaps. Nothing is buried in the wrong place. When a bug appears or a requirement changes, you know exactly where to look and fixing one thing doesn't break five others.
3. Readability: Code that explains itself

Patterns give developers a shared vocabulary. When someone reads Observer or Strategy in your code, they immediately understand what is happening no long comments, no lengthy explanations. New teammates get up to speed faster. Code reviews become smoother.
4. Flexibility: Ready for change before change arrives

Good patterns are built around loose coupling and clean abstractions. Adding a new payment method, introducing logging, or supporting a new export format becomes straightforward. You plug in something new without touching what already works.
Patterns don't just make your code work.
They make it easy to understand, safe to change, and built to last.
3. Where Do Design Patterns Come From?
blocks.text: 3. Where Do Design Patterns Come From?

blocks.content: Design patterns were popularized by four authors Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides known as the "Gang of Four" (GoF). In 1994, they published a book called Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software that changed how developers think about software design.
They documented 23 patterns that kept appearing across real-world projects. Those 23 patterns are still the foundation of design pattern education today.
4. Categories of Design Patterns
The Gang of Four organized all 23 patterns into three categories based on the type of problem they solve.
1. Creational Patterns: How objects are created
These patterns control object creation. Instead of calling new directly everywhere, they give you smarter, more flexible ways to build objects.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245772777-c62c5d68.jpg
2. Structural Patterns: How objects are composed
These patterns deal with how classes and objects fit together into larger, flexible structures.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245772923-7ea9e6b2.jpg
3. Behavioral Patterns: How objects communicate
These patterns define how objects interact and how responsibilities are distributed between them.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245773049-fc922da5.jpg
5. Think Before You Pattern
Design patterns are not universally loved and the criticisms are worth understanding before you dive in.

The first complaint is that patterns are just workarounds for language limitations. There is truth here. Some patterns only exist because older languages lacked certain features. A Python module is already a singleton. A simple lambda can replace an entire Strategy class. As languages evolve, some patterns quietly become obsolete.

The second criticism is over-engineering. This one is common and painful to watch. Developers who just learned patterns sometimes reach for a Factory or an Abstract Factory just to create a simple object adding layers of indirection that make the code harder to read than before. The pattern becomes the problem, not the solution.

The third criticism is that patterns are dated. The Gang of Four book was written in 1994. Some patterns like Interpreter are rarely implemented manually today. Iterator is built into every modern language. Functional programming has replaced many behavioral patterns entirely with simpler, more expressive alternatives.

None of this makes patterns worthless. It just means you need the right mindset going in. Understand the problem first, not the pattern name. Apply a pattern only when it genuinely makes your design cleaner and clearer. And always ask yourself is a simple, straightforward solution better here?

Patterns are tools. The goal was never to use as many as possible. The goal is to write code that is easy to understand, easy to change, and built to last. Keep that in mind, and patterns become incredibly powerful. Forget it, and they become a burden.
6. A Pattern Is a Template, Not Finished Code
blocks.text: 6. A Pattern Is a Template, Not Finished Code

blocks.content: It is worth being explicit about something the recipe analogy only hinted at. A design pattern is not a class you download and drop into your project. It has no fixed syntax, no single correct implementation, and no file you can copy from one codebase into another and expect to compile.
Why You Cannot Just Paste It In
blocks.text: Why You Cannot Just Paste It In

blocks.content: The Gang of Four book describes the Observer pattern in about four pages of prose and diagrams. It does not ship a class called Observer.java that works everywhere. That is because the shape of the solution changes depending on your language, your existing class hierarchy, and the specific relationship you are modeling.

A Singleton in a language with built in module caching looks nothing like a Singleton in a language without it. An Observer built for a UI framework will have different plumbing than one built for a stock ticker. The pattern gives you the roles and the relationships. You still have to write the code that fits your situation.
What You Actually Reuse
What transfers from project to project is not the code. It is the thinking.

["The problem the pattern is meant to solve, so you recognize it when it shows up again","The roles involved, such as a subject and its observers, or a target and an adapter","The relationships between those roles, and which one depends on which","The tradeoffs, so you know what you are gaining and what you are giving up"]
items: The problem the pattern is meant to solve, so you recognize it when it shows up again
The roles involved, such as a subject and its observers, or a target and an adapter
The relationships between those roles, and which one depends on which
The tradeoffs, so you know what you are gaining and what you are giving up

blocks.content: Once you understand those four things, writing the actual code is the easy part. You are no longer solving the problem for the first time. You are just typing out a solution you already understand.
7. The Three Categories at a Glance
blocks.text: 7. The Three Categories at a Glance

blocks.content: Before the chapters ahead go deep on individual patterns, it helps to see the three Gang of Four categories side by side, along with one representative pattern from each.

{"headers":["Category","What It Governs","Example Pattern"],"rows":[["Creational","How objects get created","Singleton"],["Structural","How objects and classes are composed","Adapter"],["Behavioral","How objects communicate and share responsibility","Observer"]]}
Every pattern you learn from here on falls into one of these three buckets. When you forget what a pattern does, remembering its category is often enough to jog your memory of its purpose.
8. Recognizing a Pattern Speeds Up Reading Code
blocks.text: 8. Recognizing a Pattern Speeds Up Reading Code

blocks.content: There is a payoff to learning patterns that has nothing to do with writing new code. It shows up the moment you open someone else's codebase.
Spotting the Shape Instead of Reading Line by Line
blocks.text: Spotting the Shape Instead of Reading Line by Line

blocks.content: Unfamiliar code is slow to read line by line. You track variables, guess at intent, and build a mental model one statement at a time. Recognizing a pattern skips most of that work. The moment you notice a class that wraps another class and forwards calls to it with small changes, you do not need to trace every method. You already know you are looking at a Decorator, and you already know roughly why it exists.
This is the same shortcut an experienced reader uses on prose. You do not sound out every letter. You recognize whole words, then whole sentence shapes. Patterns give you that same shortcut for code.

blocks.title: Walking Into an Unfamiliar Codebase
blocks.text: You open a new repository and find a class with a private constructor, a static field holding its own instance, and a public static method that returns that instance. You do not need to read the rest of the file to know what it does. You have seen a Singleton before, so you already understand the intent, the tradeoffs, and the likely reason someone reached for it here.

blocks.content: Why This Matters More as Codebases Grow
blocks.text: Why This Matters More as Codebases Grow

blocks.content: On a small script, this shortcut barely matters. On a codebase with hundreds of files built by a team over several years, it is the difference between spending a day orienting yourself and spending an hour. Pattern recognition is one of the fastest ways to get productive in code you did not write.
Now let's get into the patterns themselves.
